bread-wheat-or-cracked-wheat-reduced-cal.title: Bread made from wheat or cracked wheat, reduced calorie and/or high fiber

content.title: About
content.content: Bread made from whole wheat or cracked wheat is a whole‑grain loaf prepared with flour from intact wheat kernels or with coarse wheat groats. The reduced‑calorie version contains less fat and sugar, while the high‑fiber version is enriched with additional dietary fiber, making it more filling and beneficial for digestion.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain bread retains the bran and germ, giving it more nutrients than white bread.
Cracked wheat (also known as bulgur) has been a staple in traditional diets of many cultures, including ancient Roman and medieval cuisines.
High‑fiber bread can help stabilize blood sugar levels.
Reduced‑calorie formulations often use alternative sweeteners and lower fat content to cut calories.
Fiber increases satiety, helping with weight management.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy bowel movements, promotes regularity, and feeds beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Lower calorie content
items.content: Fewer calories aid in maintaining an energy balance during weight loss.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole wheat provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The bread supplies magnesium, iron, and zinc, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Fiber and low saturated fat content help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Wheat allergy or gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may experience serious reactions to this bread.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Because it is made from wheat, the bread is not suitable for a gluten‑free diet.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Some varieties may contain higher salt; individuals with hypertension should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bread can be enjoyed on its own, used for sandwiches, toasted for breakfast, served alongside soups, or as a base for open‑face toppings. Toasting enhances flavor and creates a pleasant crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the loaf in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or bread box. For longer storage, freeze the bread and allow it to thaw at room temperature before use.

energy-drink-sugar-free-mountain-dew-amp.title: Energy drink, sugar free (Mountain Dew AMP)

content.title: About
content.content: Mountain Dew AMP is a sugar‑free carbonated energy drink containing caffeine, taurine, B‑vitamins and artificial sweeteners. It is formulated to boost alertness, concentration and physical endurance without added sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: AMP stands for “Advanced Molecular Performance”.
The drink was first launched in the United States in 2001 as a response to the growing demand for sugar‑free energy beverages.
It contains 150 mg of caffeine per 12 oz (355 ml), roughly the amount in a strong cup of coffee.
B‑vitamins (B3, B6, B12) help support the body’s energy metabolism.
The sweetness comes from sucralose and acesulfame‑K, not from sugar.

items.title: Increased alertness
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving focus and reducing perceived fatigue.

items.title: Metabolic support
items.content: B‑vitamins assist in converting carbohydrates, fats and proteins into usable energy.

items.title: Enhanced physical endurance
items.content: Taurine may help muscles use energy more efficiently during exercise.

items.title: No sugar spike
items.content: Provides an energy boost without raising blood glucose, which is beneficial for sugar‑conscious individuals.

items.title: Excessive caffeine intake
items.content: High doses can cause anxiety, insomnia, rapid heartbeat and elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of stimulants and diminish the efficacy of sedatives.

items.title: Individual intolerance
items.content: Some people are sensitive to taurine or artificial sweeteners and may experience gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Not for children or pregnant women
items.content: Due to its caffeine content, the drink is not recommended for persons under 18, pregnant or nursing women.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Consume one 12‑oz can 30‑60 minutes before physical activity or when energy levels drop. Do not exceed 2‑3 cans per day. Avoid mixing with alcohol.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Lean pork steak is a cut taken from the low‑fat parts of the pig, such as the tenderloin or loin. It contains minimal intramuscular fat, is high in protein, and is often used in diet‑focused meals. When cooked properly it stays juicy and tender.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lean pork provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g.
Compared with beef, pork cooks faster and needs less time on the grill.
In traditional Russian cuisine, lean pork cuts were used for kotleti and baked dishes.
Pork is a good source of B‑vitamins, especially thiamine (B1), which supports the nervous system.
When stored correctly in the fridge, a lean steak stays fresh for 3‑4 days.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Protein is essential for muscle growth, repair, and immune function.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Lean pork fits well into calorie‑controlled and low‑saturated‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin and B6 aid metabolism and support nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Pork supplies zinc, iron and phosphorus, important for bone health and immunity.

items.title: Creatine content
items.content: Creatine improves muscular energy metabolism, beneficial for intense training.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Raw or undercooked pork may contain Salmonella or Trichinella; cook to an internal temperature of 63 °C.

items.title: Sodium in processed cuts
items.content: If the steak is pre‑marinated it can be high in sodium, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Rare, but some individuals may have a food allergy to pork proteins.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: People with gout should limit intake of lean pork.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lean pork steak is best grilled, pan‑seared, or baked. Slice thinly for salads, add to vegetable stews, or use in sandwiches. Finish with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or a light soy glaze for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the steak in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a vacuum‑sealed bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature, before cooking.

pretzels-soft-ready-to-eat-topped-with-c.title: Soft Pretzels, Ready‑to‑Eat, Topped with Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: Soft, ready‑to‑eat pretzels topped with cheese are a crunchy‑yet‑tender snack. The dough is baked without a long baking time, then coated with grated cheese that melts into a flavorful crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheese‑covered pretzels are often served in bars and snack shops as a quick bite.
Traditional German pretzels are boiled in a lye solution, but soft versions usually skip this step.
The cheese layer can include various cheeses – from cheddar to parmesan – depending on taste preferences.
In the United States, soft cheese pretzels gained popularity in the early 2000s with the rise of convenient snack demand.
Spice variations such as paprika or garlic powder are sometimes added to enhance flavor.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The cheese topping adds both dairy and animal protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Cheese is rich in calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese provides B2 and B12 vitamins, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: The pretzel dough supplies carbohydrates for rapid energy.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: When whole‑grain flour is used in the dough, fiber content increases, benefiting digestion.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The cheese layer can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with dairy allergies or lactose intolerance.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Cheese‑covered pretzels often contain a notable amount of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Combined dough and cheese make these snacks calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: The cheese adds saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed excessively.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pretzels are convenient as a stand‑alone snack, paired with dips (such as mustard or tomato), or served alongside beer. They can be briefly warmed in a microwave to make the cheese more melty.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 5 days. For longer storage, refrigerate – up to 2 weeks. Discard if any mold appears or the smell changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Pupusa is a traditional Salvadoran dish consisting of a thin corn‑maize tortilla filled with seasoned meat and beans. The dough, made from masa (finely ground corn flour), is cooked until soft yet sturdy, creating a pocket that holds the savory filling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pupusas are often served with curtido (pickled cabbage) and salsa roja, which add tangy contrast.
Traditionally they are cooked on a flat griddle called a “comal” over an open flame.
In El Salvador, pupusas are a national staple and are featured in festivals and family gatherings.
There are many filling variations, from cheese and spinach to seafood; meat with beans is one of the most popular.
The corn masa provides complex carbohydrates that give lasting energy.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat filling supplies high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Beans and corn masa add soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and beans provide B6, B12, and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish offers iron, zinc, and magnesium, contributing to immune health and energy production.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: Pupusas are naturally low in sugar, making them suitable for balanced carbohydrate intake.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to corn masa used in the tortilla.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: If the filling is seasoned with salty sauces, the dish can be high in sodium.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Meat‑and‑bean pupusas are relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor harmful bacteria; ensure the filling reaches a safe internal temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pupusas are served hot, usually split in half. Eat them with your hands, topping with salsa, sour cream, grated cheese, or avocado. For a fresher bite, add sliced tomatoes, lettuce, or pickled onions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pupusas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. They can be frozen wrapped tightly in plastic and later reheated on a skillet or in the microwave.

rice-white-with-other-vegetables-no-adde.title: White Rice with Vegetables, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: White rice cooked together with a mix of vegetables (carrot, broccoli, peas) without any added fat. It is a light dish rich in carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals, suitable for a balanced diet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice is one of the most consumed grains worldwide, cultivated in over 100 countries.
Combining rice with vegetables boosts dietary fiber and B‑vitamin content.
Cooking without fat preserves the natural flavors of the vegetables.
White rice has a higher glycemic index than whole grain rice, but the presence of vegetables moderates its impact.
Rice with vegetables is a staple in many Asian cuisines, often served as a basic meal.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbohydrates.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium, and magnesium, supporting immunity and muscle function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables increase the fiber content, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Vegetables contain a high water percentage, helping maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: Rare but possible allergic reactions to rice may occur.

items.title: Lack of fat
items.content: Without fat, the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins from the vegetables may be reduced; consider adding a small amount of healthy fat elsewhere in the diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a standalone dish or as a side to meat, fish, or tofu. Add soy sauce, fresh herbs, or a squeeze of lemon for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Freeze for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Steak teriyaki is a piece of beef marinated in a teriyaki sauce made from soy sauce, mirin, sugar and ginger, then quickly seared over high heat. The result is tender meat with a sweet‑salty aroma characteristic of Asian cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Teriyaki originates from Japan, where the sauce was used to give dishes a glossy, slightly sweet flavor.
Traditional teriyaki sauce is made without corn starch, though many commercial versions use thickeners.
Marinating beef in teriyaki sauce enhances flavor and makes the meat more tender.
In Japan, steak teriyaki is often served with rice, vegetables, and a sprinkle of sesame seeds.
There is a pineapple‑infused teriyaki variation that adds extra sweetness and aroma.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The iron in beef is highly bioavailable and helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Steak teriyaki supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from soy sauce
items.content: Soy sauce in the teriyaki glaze contains phenolic compounds with antioxidant activity.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Ginger and garlic, often added to teriyaki, have anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce is salty, so people with hypertension should limit portion size.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Teriyaki sauce is frequently sweetened, which can increase the dish’s calorie count.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy sauce.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Commercial sauces may contain preservatives and flavor enhancers that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Marinate the steak in teriyaki sauce for at least 30 minutes (up to 4 hours). Then sear it on a hot pan or grill for 2–3 minutes per side to the desired doneness. Let the meat rest for 5 minutes, slice thinly, and serve with rice, vegetables or a salad, sprinkled with sesame seeds.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked steak teriyaki in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Uncooked beef in the marinade can be kept in the fridge for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, freeze in a separate bag; it will retain quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Tofu is a soy curd made from soy milk. In this dish tofu is combined with carrots, broccoli and/or dark‑green leafy vegetables, dressed with a soy‑based sauce. The meal is rich in plant protein, fiber, vitamins and minerals, and contains no potatoes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tofu has a neutral flavor, allowing it to absorb the taste of sauces and spices easily.
Broccoli contains sulforaphane, a compound studied for its potential anti‑cancer properties.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables such as spinach and kale are high in vitamin K and antioxidants.
Soy sauce (2242) is a traditional Japanese condiment produced by fermenting soybeans, wheat, salt and water.
The combination of tofu and vegetables provides a complete set of essential amino acids.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Tofu supplies all essential amino acids, making it a valuable protein source for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Dark‑green leafy vegetables and soy sauce provide calcium, magnesium and vitamin K, which contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Broccoli and carrots are abundant in beta‑carotene and vitamin C, helping combat free radicals.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables promotes intestinal motility and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The absence of potatoes and the presence of tofu make the dish suitable for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy products, including tofu and soy sauce.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce can be high in salt; people monitoring sodium intake should use it in moderation.

items.title: Phytates
items.content: Soybeans contain phytates, which may reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut tofu into cubes and lightly sauté, then add boiled or steamed vegetables. Drizzle the mixture with soy sauce (2242) and, if desired, sprinkle with sesame seeds. It can be served hot or cold, as a salad topping or as a side dish to grains.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tofu in an airtight container, covered with fresh water and change the water daily; keep it in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Keep vegetables in a separate bag in the crisper drawer. Soy sauce should be kept in a cool, dark place and refrigerated after opening.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta is pasta made from whole wheat flour or other whole grains, so it keeps the bran and germ. It has a chewier texture, a nuttier flavor, and a darker color than regular pasta. Whole grain pasta is cooked and served like regular pasta in a wide range of dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta is made with flour that includes the bran, germ, and endosperm of the grain.
It has a chewier texture and a nuttier flavor than pasta made from refined flour.
Whole grain pasta also comes in versions made from other grains, such as spelt, brown rice, and whole oats, and blends.
Pasta is traditionally made from durum wheat, which is high in protein.
Cooking pasta al dente, which means firm to the bite, keeps its texture and lowers its glycemic effect.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains more fiber than regular pasta, which supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains manganese, magnesium, selenium, and phosphorus.

items.title: Contains B vitamins
items.content: Whole grain pasta provides niacin and thiamin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Slower-digesting carbohydrates
items.content: Whole grain pasta cooked al dente raises blood sugar more slowly.

items.title: Provides plant protein
items.content: Pasta provides protein, especially when made from durum wheat.

items.title: Gluten and wheat allergy
items.content: Whole grain pasta made from wheat contains gluten and should be avoided by people with celiac disease, gluten sensitivity, or wheat allergy.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: The higher fiber content may cause gas or bloating in some people, especially if increased quickly.

items.title: Portion size and sauces
items.content: Pasta can be high in calories, especially with creamy or oily sauces, so portion size matters.

items.title: Texture and taste
items.content: Some people find whole grain pasta tougher or slightly bitter, and it can turn mushy if overcooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whole grain pasta can be boiled in plenty of salted water until al dente and served with tomato sauce, vegetables, legumes, fish, or olive oil and garlic. It works well in pasta salads and baked dishes. Pair it with vegetables and protein, and choose bolder sauces that suit its nutty flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry whole grain pasta in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Because it contains the germ with its natural oils, it can keep for a shorter time than regular pasta, so use it by the date on the package. Cooked pasta should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to five days.

content.title: About
content.content: Winter melon (also known as white gourd) becomes tender and mildly sweet after cooking. It is high in water, low in calories, and provides modest amounts of B‑vitamins, vitamin C, potassium and magnesium.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Winter melon is cultivated in tropical and subtropical Asia, especially China, Thailand and India.
Raw fruits can weigh up to 50 kg, but they are usually cooked before consumption.
In traditional Chinese medicine the fruit is considered cooling and is used to help eliminate excess fluid.
In Japan cooked winter melon is used in sweet desserts such as mochi and jelly.
Its dense texture makes it a popular meat substitute in vegetarian and vegan dishes.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Cooked winter melon provides about 20 kcal per 100 g, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potassium supports fluid balance and normal heart function.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and is essential for collagen synthesis.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber in the fruit promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phytonutrients such as carotenoids help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions, including skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Winter melon contains low levels of oxalates, so people prone to kidney stones should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Possible contaminants
items.content: When grown under poor conditions, pesticide residues may be present; choose organic or wash thoroughly before cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked winter melon can be diced and added to soups, stews, curries or salads. It is also used to make purees, casseroles and sweet desserts such as jelly or mousse.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked winter melon in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4‑5 days. For longer keeping, freeze it in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months.
